story.title: Homeland Security Leak Exposes More Than 41,000 Employees - The New York Times

facts.text: “DHS is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively,” a Homeland Security spokesperson tells WIRED.
ICE accounts for about 10,000, roughly a third of them in Homeland Security Investigations, ICE’s investigative wing.

Noem, McCord, Hegseth, and Krachenfels did not respond to a request for comment Other groups named in the leak reference AI tools, including OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Google’s Gemini, and Microsoft’s Copilot.
The leak follows a breach in which a group of hackers known as ShinyHunters claimed to have stolen personal information on nearly every FBI employee and their families.
“We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected.

This is the latest data breach to hit the U.S. government in recent months, following earlier hacks involving the theft of thousands of FBI agents’ personnel records and the personal information of millions of serving and former military service personnel from the Pentagon’s human resources unit .
TechCrunch verified a portion of the data as authentic by matching the names of several known Homeland Security employees against an offline copy of the database.
The number of leaked records is equivalent to about one-fifth of Homeland Security’s workforce, which totals around 220,000 staff .
Critics have called for investigations into tech companies that fund or provide their technology to ICE.
A spokesperson for Homeland Security told TechCrunch after publication: “DHS is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively.
We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected.
We will update the public when more information is available.”
The Okta system also contains IT and log-in records associated with the employees’ user account, including details about which systems and internal apps they are permitted to access.
Penlink has had a contract with ICE for years.
One group specifically references Penlink PLX, which the company says is used to capture and analyze “real-time intelligence” from phone calls, texts, web activity, and social media.

One user group also includes more than 200 CBP users associated with Mobile Fortify, a facial-recognition app used by both CBP and ICE agents to identify people and verify their information and immigration status .

The stolen Homeland Security data was provided to journalist and hacker maia arson crimew, who then shared a copy with DDoSecrets , a nonprofit collective that hosts leaked datasets in the public interest.
“They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs,” said Department of Peace in a note left with the data, which TechCrunch has seen.
The hacker did not respond to TechCrunch’s email requesting comment and with questions about how the breach was carried out.
Zack Whittaker is the security editor at TechCrunch.
More than half of the dataset — some 21,000 records — relate to employees with U.S.
Customs and Border Protection (CBP), who work at airports and other ports of entry.

The user groups also include several employees associated with ChatGPT access, including senior DHS officials, as well as other groups associated with investigations into the China-backed hacking groups known as Salt Typhoon and Volt Typhoon.

The leaked data contains information about employees’ membership in user groups within the department’s Active Directory, a system that controls access to the department’s internal tools, services, and third-party offerings used for work.
The Washington Post said a hacking group published a searchable database containing more than 41,000 employees and contractors of the U.S.
Department of Homeland Security, exposing the identities and contact information of immigration officials, border patrol agents, and undercover investigators.

The nonprofit site said it based the disclosure on information obtained by an entity calling itself the Ministry of Peace, and the leak was described as the third-largest government data leak to make headlines in the past month.

Washington: A nonprofit news leak group said Wednesday it has published data on more than 41,000 employees of the US Department of Homeland Security, including those working on President Donald Trump's immigration enforcement efforts.

Distributed Denial of Secrets (DDOS) said it obtained the sensitive information from a "hacktivist group" known as the Department of Peace, which created a tool named Icepick that facilitates detailed searches of employee names, offices and assignments.
